dx: Wernicke encephalopathy progressing to Korsakoff syndrome
case: A 47-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by police after he was found confused in a park. He has alcohol use disorder and has eaten little for several weeks. His temperature is 36.4 °C (97.5 °F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. He is disoriented to place and time and cannot keep his attention on the examiner. There is horizontal nystagmus with bilateral weakness of abduction. He walks with a wide-based, staggering gait and cannot walk heel to toe. Finger-to-nose testing and rapid alternating hand movements are normal. Serum glucose is 68 mg/dL (reference 70 to 100 mg/dL). Diagnosis: Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine deficiency.

questions.stem: He receives thiamine but recovers only partly. Over the following months he cannot retain new information for more than a few minutes, and when asked what he did yesterday he gives detailed accounts of events that never happened. He dies 4 years later. Which of the following is most likely to be found at autopsy?
options: Neuronal loss in the hippocampal CA1 sector
Pallor of the substantia nigra pars compacta
Atrophy of the head of the caudate nucleus
approach: Name the new syndrome: anterograde amnesia with confabulation after Wernicke encephalopathy is Korsakoff syndrome.
Recall where thiamine deficiency injures the brain: mammillary bodies, medial (dorsomedial) thalamus, and the gray matter around the third ventricle and aqueduct.
Pick the chronic lesion of those structures.
questions.why: Thiamine deficiency damages the mammillary bodies, the dorsomedial thalamic nuclei, and periventricular and periaqueductal gray matter. Acute lesions show petechial hemorrhages and capillary proliferation. Over time the mammillary bodies shrink and turn brown from old hemosiderin. Damage to the mammillary bodies and medial thalamus breaks the memory circuit, which causes the lasting anterograde amnesia and confabulation of Korsakoff syndrome.
whyNot: CA1 neurons die after global hypoxia, such as cardiac arrest. That causes amnesia, but confabulation after Wernicke encephalopathy points to mammillary and thalamic damage.
Nigral pallor is the gross finding in Parkinson disease, which causes tremor, rigidity, and slow movement.
Correct.
Caudate atrophy is the hallmark of Huntington disease, which causes chorea and dementia.

questions.stem: Because of his low glucose, emergency staff give an infusion of 5% dextrose before any thiamine is given. Over the next hour his confusion deepens, and serum lactate rises to 4.6 mmol/L (reference 0.5 to 2.2 mmol/L). Reduced activity of which of the following enzymes best explains these changes?
approach: Identify the deficient cofactor: thiamine pyrophosphate.
List the enzymes that need it: pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, and transketolase.
A glucose load pushes more pyruvate toward pyruvate dehydrogenase. When that step is blocked, pyruvate is turned into lactate and the brain makes less ATP.
questions.why: Thiamine pyrophosphate is the cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase, which links glycolysis to the citric acid cycle. The brain runs almost entirely on glucose oxidation, so it depends heavily on this step. Giving glucose to a thiamine-deficient patient raises the flow of pyruvate into a blocked enzyme. Pyruvate backs up and is converted to lactate, and neurons in vulnerable areas run short of ATP. This is why thiamine is given before or with glucose in malnourished patients.
whyNot: Correct.
Pyruvate carboxylase uses biotin, not thiamine. It makes oxaloacetate for gluconeogenesis.
Lactate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate to lactate and needs no thiamine. It is working harder here, which is why lactate rises.
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase starts the pentose phosphate pathway and uses NADP+, not thiamine. Transketolase is the thiamine-dependent enzyme of that pathway.

questions.stem: Position sense in his toes is normal, and he sways just as much with his eyes open as with them closed. Damage to which of the following structures best explains his gait disturbance?
options: Dorsal columns of the spinal cord
approach: Separate sensory ataxia from cerebellar ataxia: normal position sense and no worsening with eyes closed rule out a dorsal column cause.
Note that the trunk and gait are affected while arm coordination is normal.
Midline (vermis) lesions cause truncal and gait ataxia; hemisphere lesions cause limb ataxia on the same side.
questions.why: The cerebellar vermis controls the axial and proximal muscles used for posture and walking. Damage to it gives a wide-based, unsteady gait with truncal sway, while finger-to-nose testing can stay normal. In alcohol use disorder and thiamine deficiency, the anterior superior vermis is the part most often damaged. Lateral hemisphere lesions instead cause intention tremor, dysmetria, and dysdiadochokinesia in the limbs on the same side.
whyNot: Dorsal column damage causes sensory ataxia with lost position sense and a positive Romberg sign, where sway worsens with the eyes closed. His position sense is normal.
The dentate nuclei receive output from the lateral hemispheres. Damage causes limb ataxia and intention tremor, but his hand coordination is normal.
Hemisphere lesions cause ipsilateral limb ataxia, intention tremor, and dysdiadochokinesia. His finger-to-nose and rapid alternating movements are normal.
Correct.

questions.stem: Three years later, he has chronic pancreatitis with greasy, foul-smelling stools. He now has worsening ataxia of his limbs and gait, loss of vibration and position sense in both feet, and absent ankle reflexes. Serum vitamin B12 and methylmalonic acid concentrations are within the reference ranges. Deficiency of which of the following is the most likely cause of these new findings?
approach: Greasy stools from pancreatic insufficiency mean fat malabsorption, so think of fat-soluble vitamins.
Ataxia with dorsal column loss and neuropathy, with normal B12 and methylmalonic acid, matches vitamin E deficiency.
Rule out the water-soluble vitamins by their own neurologic patterns.
questions.why: Vitamin E (alpha-tocopherol) is a fat-soluble antioxidant that protects the lipid-rich membranes of neurons from oxidative injury. Fat malabsorption from chronic pancreatitis, cholestasis, or cystic fibrosis can deplete it. Deficiency damages the spinocerebellar tracts, dorsal columns, and peripheral nerves, giving ataxia, loss of vibration and position sense, and areflexia. It looks like B12 deficiency, but B12 and methylmalonic acid are normal and there is no megaloblastic anemia.
whyNot: Vitamin A is also fat soluble, but deficiency causes night blindness, dry eyes, and dry skin, not ataxia.
Correct.
Niacin deficiency causes pellagra: dermatitis on sun-exposed skin, diarrhea, and dementia. It does not cause dorsal column loss.
Pyridoxine deficiency causes peripheral neuropathy, as with isoniazid use, and seizures in infants. It is water soluble, so fat malabsorption is not its typical cause.

dx: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) with early-onset Alzheimer disease
case: A 46-year-old man with Down syndrome is brought to the physician by his sister because of 2 years of worsening memory. He used to work part time and dress himself, but he now gets lost in his own neighborhood and needs help with daily tasks. His karyotype at birth was 47,XY,+21, and an atrioventricular septal defect was repaired in infancy. Examination shows upslanting palpebral fissures, a flat facial profile, single palmar creases, and mild generalized hypotonia. He is oriented to person only. MRI of the brain shows diffuse cortical atrophy, most marked in the hippocampi. Diagnosis: Down syndrome with early-onset Alzheimer disease.

questions.stem: He needs general anesthesia for a dental procedure. Before intubation, the anesthesiologist asks about neck symptoms and avoids forceful neck extension. Which of the following complications of his condition is the main concern?
options: Fusion of cervical vertebrae from failed segmentation
Chiari I herniation of the cerebellar tonsils
approach: Recall the musculoskeletal features of Down syndrome: generalized ligament laxity and hypotonia.
Laxity of the transverse ligament lets C1 slide on C2.
Forced neck extension or flexion during intubation can then compress the upper cervical cord.
questions.why: About 1 in 10 to 1 in 5 people with Down syndrome have extra movement between C1 and C2 because the transverse ligament that holds the dens is lax. Most have no symptoms, but sudden neck movement, as during intubation or contact sports, can compress the cord. Warning signs include neck pain, a new gait change, weakness, and bladder change. Down syndrome also brings intellectual disability, hypotonia, early Alzheimer disease, AV septal defects, duodenal atresia, and a higher risk of acute leukemia.
whyNot: Correct.
Congenital fusion of cervical vertebrae is Klippel-Feil syndrome, which is not a feature of Down syndrome.
Chiari I malformation is not part of Down syndrome. It presents with occipital headache worse with coughing and may cause a syrinx.
Syringomyelia is linked to Chiari I malformation and cord trauma, not to Down syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why he developed Alzheimer disease decades earlier than is typical in the general population?
options: Prion protein gene mutation on chromosome 20
Third copy of the APP gene on chromosome 21
approach: Link his karyotype, 47,XY,+21, to a third copy of every gene on chromosome 21.
Recall that the amyloid precursor protein (APP) gene is on chromosome 21.
More APP means more beta-amyloid, so plaques form decades early.
questions.why: The APP gene sits on chromosome 21. With three copies, cells make about 1.5 times the normal amount of APP, and more is cut into beta-amyloid. Plaques appear in most people with Down syndrome by about age 40, and dementia often follows in the 40s and 50s. Most trisomy 21 comes from maternal meiotic nondisjunction, and risk rises with maternal age. A smaller share comes from a Robertsonian translocation or from mosaicism.
whyNot: Presenilin 1 mutations cause autosomal dominant early-onset Alzheimer disease, but they are not part of trisomy 21.
The E4 allele raises Alzheimer risk in the general population and is common in late-onset disease. It does not explain the near-universal early pathology in Down syndrome.
Prion protein gene mutations cause familial prion diseases such as familial Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, which progress over months.
Correct.

topics: APP gene dosage and Alzheimer disease

questions.stem: Because thyroid disease is common in his condition and can worsen cognition, serum TSH is measured and is 14 μU/mL (reference 0.5 to 5.0 μU/mL). His ankle reflexes show a normal contraction followed by a slow return to the resting position. Which of the following best explains the slow relaxation phase?
options: Reduced acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction
Slower calcium reuptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Demyelination that slows the afferent limb of the reflex
Loss of upper motor neuron inhibition of the reflex arc
approach: Read the high TSH as primary hypothyroidism.
Note that only relaxation is slow, so the problem lies in the muscle after contraction, not in the nerve.
Thyroid hormone drives expression of the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium pump; less pump activity means slower relaxation.
questions.why: Muscle relaxes when calcium is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum by the SERCA ATPase. Thyroid hormone increases SERCA expression and speeds both contraction and relaxation. In hypothyroidism, calcium is cleared slowly, so the reflex has a delayed relaxation phase. Hyperthyroidism does the reverse, with brisk reflexes and tremor. In infants, untreated congenital hypothyroidism impairs brain development, which is why newborns are screened.
whyNot: Reduced acetylcholine release, as in Lambert-Eaton syndrome, weakens contraction. It does not slow relaxation.
Correct.
Slow afferent conduction would delay the start of the reflex and weaken it. The contraction here is normal.
Upper motor neuron loss makes reflexes brisk with spread and clonus. It does not slow relaxation.

questions.stem: He is also found to have bilateral cataracts, which are common in adults with his condition. Cataracts can also develop in the first weeks of life from an inherited metabolic disorder. A 3-week-old boy is brought to the physician because of vomiting and jaundice that began in his first week of breastfeeding. Physical examination shows hepatomegaly, and slit-lamp examination shows bilateral lens opacities. His urine contains a reducing substance that is not glucose. Accumulation of which of the following in the lens most directly causes the cataracts in this infant?
approach: Link illness after starting milk, liver disease, and a non-glucose reducing sugar to classic galactosemia.
Excess galactose is reduced in the lens by aldose reductase.
The sugar alcohol formed is trapped in lens cells, draws in water, and makes the lens proteins opaque.
questions.why: In classic galactosemia, galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase is missing, so galactose and galactose-1-phosphate build up. In the lens, aldose reductase reduces galactose to galactitol. Galactitol cannot leave the cell, so water follows it in, the fibers swell, and lens proteins lose their clear order. The same process with glucose and sorbitol explains cataracts in diabetes. Other cataract risks include age, corticosteroids, UV light, smoking, and congenital rubella.
whyNot: Sorbitol is made from glucose by aldose reductase and causes cataracts in diabetes, not in galactosemia.

Galactose-1-phosphate builds up in classic galactosemia and injures the liver, kidney, and brain, but the lens damage comes from galactitol. Galactokinase deficiency causes cataracts without this metabolite.
Correct.
Fructose-1-phosphate builds up in hereditary fructose intolerance, which causes hypoglycemia and liver injury after fruit or sucrose, not cataracts.

case: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the physician because his school performance has fallen over 6 months. His teacher reports trouble following directions and copying from the board, and he has become clumsy. He tires easily. His maternal uncle died at the age of 9 years of a progressive neurologic illness. Examination shows dark skin in the palmar creases and over the knuckles, brisk reflexes in the legs, and difficulty with fine motor tasks. MRI of the brain shows symmetric T2 hyperintensity in the parieto-occipital white matter with an enhancing leading edge. Plasma very long chain fatty acid levels are elevated. Diagnosis: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.

questions.stem: Which of the following defects most directly explains the accumulation of very long chain fatty acids in this patient?
approach: Recall where very long chain fatty acids are broken down: peroxisomes, not mitochondria.
X-linked inheritance through the mother's side and adrenal involvement point to the ABCD1 gene.
ABCD1 encodes a peroxisomal membrane transporter that brings these fatty acids in for beta-oxidation.
questions.why: Fatty acids with 22 or more carbons are shortened by beta-oxidation inside peroxisomes. In X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy, mutations in ABCD1 disable the transporter that carries them across the peroxisomal membrane. The fatty acids build up in myelin, the adrenal cortex, and the testes. In the childhood cerebral form, this triggers inflammatory demyelination that usually starts in the parieto-occipital white matter, along with adrenal insufficiency.
whyNot: Arylsulfatase A deficiency is metachromatic leukodystrophy, an autosomal recessive disease in which sulfatides build up. Fatty acid levels are normal.
Galactocerebrosidase deficiency is Krabbe disease, an autosomal recessive infantile leukodystrophy with globoid cells. It does not affect the adrenal glands.
The carnitine shuttle moves long chain fatty acids into mitochondria. Defects cause hypoketotic hypoglycemia and muscle weakness with fasting.
Correct.

questions.stem: His 8 AM serum cortisol is 2 μg/dL (reference 5 to 25 μg/dL), and his plasma ACTH is 480 pg/mL (reference 10 to 60 pg/mL). Which of the following best explains the darkening of his skin?
options: Lost cortisol feedback raising ACTH output
Excess aldosterone acting on skin melanocytes
Reduced dopamine inhibition of the pituitary
approach: Low cortisol with high ACTH means the problem is in the adrenal cortex (primary adrenal insufficiency).
Cortisol normally inhibits CRH release from the hypothalamus and ACTH release from the pituitary.
Without that feedback, ACTH rises, and ACTH stimulates melanocortin 1 receptors on melanocytes.
questions.why: The HPA axis runs from CRH in the paraventricular nucleus to ACTH in the anterior pituitary to cortisol in the adrenal cortex, and cortisol feeds back to shut off the first two steps. When the adrenal cortex fails, feedback is lost and pituitary corticotrophs make large amounts of proopiomelanocortin (POMC), the precursor that is cut into ACTH. ACTH binds melanocortin 1 receptors on melanocytes and stimulates melanin production. The result is darkening of creases, knuckles, and mucosa. The other arm of the stress response, sympathetic output to the adrenal medulla, is not the cause of skin change.
whyNot: The adrenal medulla releases epinephrine in response to stress through sympathetic preganglionic fibers. Catecholamines do not darken the skin.
Correct.
Aldosterone has no effect on melanocytes, and in primary adrenal insufficiency it is normal or low, not high.
Dopamine from the hypothalamus inhibits prolactin, not ACTH. Loss of dopamine raises prolactin and does not darken the skin.

questions.stem: His MRI changes reflect destruction of myelin within the cerebral white matter. The cells that formed this myelin differ from the myelinating cells of his peripheral nerves in which of the following ways?
options: Each cell myelinates internodes on many axons
Each cell myelinates one internode of one axon
Each cell arises from the neural crest
Each cell is covered by a basal lamina
approach: Identify the myelinating cell of the brain white matter: the oligodendrocyte.
Compare it with the Schwann cell of peripheral nerve.
Oligodendrocytes extend many processes, each wrapping one internode on a different axon.
questions.why: An oligodendrocyte sends out many processes, and each one wraps an internode on a separate axon, so one cell myelinates segments of many axons. A Schwann cell wraps a single internode of a single axon and is covered by a basal lamina that guides regrowth after injury. Oligodendrocytes come from neuroectoderm, while Schwann cells come from neural crest. Oligodendrocyte injury underlies multiple sclerosis, PML, and the leukodystrophies, while Schwann cell injury underlies Guillain-Barré syndrome.
whyNot: Correct.
This describes a Schwann cell in a peripheral nerve.
Schwann cells arise from neural crest. Oligodendrocytes arise from neuroectoderm of the neural tube.
Schwann cells have a basal lamina, which helps guide axon regrowth. Oligodendrocytes do not.

questions.stem: His ACTH is driven by a hypothalamic hormone that reaches the anterior pituitary through the hypophyseal portal system. If this portal connection were cut by a transection of the pituitary stalk, the serum concentration of which of the following anterior pituitary hormones would most likely rise?
approach: Recall that hypothalamic hormones reach the anterior pituitary only through portal capillaries in the stalk.
Most of these hormones are stimulatory (CRH, TRH, GnRH, GHRH), so cutting the stalk lowers the hormones they drive.
Prolactin is held down mainly by dopamine, so loss of portal dopamine lets prolactin rise.
questions.why: Hypothalamic neurons release their hormones into a capillary bed in the median eminence. Portal veins carry this blood down the stalk to a second capillary bed in the anterior pituitary. CRH, TRH, GnRH, and GHRH stimulate their target cells, while somatostatin inhibits growth hormone and TSH. Prolactin is unique because its main control is inhibitory, from dopamine made in the arcuate nucleus. Cutting or compressing the stalk removes dopamine, so prolactin rises while the other anterior pituitary hormones fall.
whyNot: ACTH depends on CRH from the hypothalamus. Losing portal flow would lower it.
Growth hormone depends mainly on GHRH. Losing portal flow would lower it.
Correct.
TSH depends on TRH. Losing portal flow would lower it.

case: A 14-month-old girl is brought to the physician because she cannot sit without support and has had several seizures. She was born at home and had no newborn screening. Her parents are first cousins. Examination shows a head circumference below the 3rd percentile, eczema on her cheeks and arms, and hair and skin much lighter than those of her parents and siblings. Her urine and sweat have a musty odor. She does not babble or reach for toys. Plasma phenylalanine is 1,450 μmol/L (reference less than 120 μmol/L), and plasma tyrosine is low-normal. Phenylalanine hydroxylase gene testing shows two pathogenic variants. Diagnosis: phenylketonuria.

questions.stem: She is started on a phenylalanine-restricted diet. At the age of 24 years, she stops the diet and becomes pregnant. Her plasma phenylalanine during pregnancy is 1,100 μmol/L. Which of the following is most likely in her infant?
options: Neural tube defect from folate antagonism
Musty odor from fetal phenylalanine hydroxylase loss
approach: Recognize maternal phenylketonuria: the mother's high phenylalanine crosses the placenta.
The fetus is exposed to toxic levels whether or not it has PKU itself.
The main effects are microcephaly, intellectual disability, growth restriction, and congenital heart disease.
questions.why: Phenylalanine is actively carried across the placenta, so fetal levels run even higher than the mother's. High levels harm the developing brain and heart. Infants of mothers with untreated PKU often have microcephaly, intellectual disability, low birth weight, and heart defects, even though most of them are only carriers. Restarting the diet before conception and keeping levels low through pregnancy prevents this. PKU itself is autosomal recessive loss of phenylalanine hydroxylase or its cofactor BH4, which makes tyrosine an essential amino acid.
whyNot: Neonatal hypoglycemia from fetal hyperinsulinism occurs in infants of mothers with poorly controlled diabetes.
Correct.
Neural tube defects follow folate deficiency or folate antagonists such as valproate. High phenylalanine damages the brain and heart instead.
The infant is most likely a carrier with one working allele, so it can clear phenylalanine after birth. The harm comes from exposure in the womb.

questions.stem: A second infant has a similar plasma phenylalanine level but normal phenylalanine hydroxylase activity. He has deficient dihydropteridine reductase, which regenerates tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4). His cerebrospinal fluid shows low homovanillic acid. Which of the following enzymes in catecholamine synthesis is most directly impaired in this infant?
approach: Low homovanillic acid means low dopamine production.
Find the catecholamine enzyme that, like phenylalanine hydroxylase, uses BH4.
Tyrosine hydroxylase converts tyrosine to L-DOPA, the rate-limiting step, and needs BH4.
questions.why: Catecholamine synthesis runs tyrosine to L-DOPA (tyrosine hydroxylase, rate limiting, BH4 dependent), L-DOPA to dopamine (aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase, pyridoxal phosphate dependent), dopamine to norepinephrine (dopamine beta-hydroxylase, vitamin C and copper dependent), and norepinephrine to epinephrine (PNMT in the adrenal medulla, induced by cortisol). Phenylalanine hydroxylase, tyrosine hydroxylase, and tryptophan hydroxylase all share BH4. So BH4 defects cause high phenylalanine plus low dopamine and serotonin, and a low-phenylalanine diet alone does not treat them.
whyNot: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase uses vitamin C and copper, not BH4. Its loss would leave dopamine and homovanillic acid normal or high.
This enzyme uses pyridoxal phosphate, not BH4.
Correct.
PNMT uses S-adenosylmethionine to make epinephrine from norepinephrine and is induced by cortisol. It does not need BH4.

questions.stem: Before treatment, her cerebrospinal fluid concentration of 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid was well below the reference range. Which of the following best explains this finding?
options: Less tryptophan reaching raphe neurons for hydroxylation
Increased monoamine oxidase activity in serotonergic terminals
Diversion of serotonin to melatonin in the pineal gland
Reduced conversion of tryptophan to niacin in the liver
approach: Identify 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid as the breakdown product of serotonin made by monoamine oxidase.
A low level means less serotonin is being made in the brain.
High phenylalanine competes with tryptophan for transport into the brain and inhibits tryptophan hydroxylase in the raphe nuclei.
questions.why: Brain serotonin is made in the raphe nuclei. Tryptophan hydroxylase converts tryptophan to 5-hydroxytryptophan, which is then decarboxylated to serotonin. Monoamine oxidase breaks serotonin down to 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid, so the CSF level tracks serotonin turnover. In untreated PKU, phenylalanine crowds tryptophan off the shared large neutral amino acid carrier at the blood-brain barrier and also inhibits tryptophan hydroxylase, so less serotonin is made. The pineal gland converts a small share of serotonin to melatonin at night.
whyNot: Correct.
More monoamine oxidase activity would raise 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid, not lower it.
The pineal gland uses only a tiny fraction of brain serotonin to make melatonin. This could not drain the whole pool.
Tryptophan conversion to niacin happens in the liver and does not set brain serotonin levels.

topics: Brain amino acid transport in PKU

questions.stem: Her mother describes the seizures. Each begins with rhythmic jerking of the right hand that spreads up the right arm over about 20 seconds. She then stops responding, and all four limbs stiffen and jerk for about 1 minute. Afterward she is sleepy for an hour. She has no fever with these episodes. Which of the following best describes these seizures?
approach: Find where the seizure starts: one hand, so it begins in one area of the left motor cortex.
Follow its spread: it moves along the motor strip, then involves both hemispheres with loss of awareness and tonic-clonic activity.
Classify by onset, then by spread: focal onset evolving to bilateral tonic-clonic.
questions.why: A seizure is excessive, synchronous firing of a group of neurons when excitation outweighs inhibition. Focal seizures start in one network of one hemisphere, so the first sign points to the starting area, here the hand region of the left motor cortex. Spread along the motor strip gives a march of jerking up the limb. When the discharge spreads to both hemispheres, the patient loses awareness and has a tonic-clonic phase, followed by postictal drowsiness. Generalized seizures involve both hemispheres from the start.
whyNot: Absence seizures are brief staring spells of a few seconds with 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges, no aura, and no postictal state.
Seizures that are generalized from onset begin with loss of awareness in both hemispheres at once. Her seizures start in one hand and spread, which marks a focal onset.
Simple febrile seizures occur with fever in children 6 months to 5 years old and are generalized from the start. She has no fever and a focal onset.
Correct.

case: An 8-month-old boy is brought to the physician because he has stopped rolling over and no longer reaches for toys. He developed normally until the age of 5 months. He startles strongly at ordinary household sounds. Both parents are healthy and are of Ashkenazi Jewish descent. Examination shows generalized hypotonia, poor head control, and brisk reflexes. Funduscopic examination shows a cherry-red spot in the center of each macula. The liver and spleen are not enlarged. Leukocyte hexosaminidase A activity is markedly reduced. Diagnosis: Tay-Sachs disease.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old girl also has developmental regression and a cherry-red spot in each macula. She has marked hepatosplenomegaly, and a bone marrow aspirate shows lipid-laden foam cells. Deficiency of which of the following enzymes is most likely in this girl?
approach: A cherry-red macula with regression narrows the choice to Tay-Sachs or Niemann-Pick disease.
Hepatosplenomegaly and foam cells mean lipid is stored in macrophages of the liver, spleen, and marrow.
That pattern fits Niemann-Pick disease, from sphingomyelinase deficiency.
questions.why: In both Tay-Sachs and Niemann-Pick type A disease, lipid stored in retinal ganglion cells around the fovea makes the macula look pale, and the fovea, which has no ganglion cells, stands out as a cherry-red spot. Tay-Sachs stores GM2 ganglioside mainly in neurons, so the liver and spleen stay normal size. Niemann-Pick type A stores sphingomyelin in neurons and in macrophages throughout the body, which gives hepatosplenomegaly and foamy marrow cells. Both are autosomal recessive and more common in people of Ashkenazi Jewish descent.
whyNot: Hexosaminidase A deficiency is Tay-Sachs disease, as in the first infant, which spares the liver and spleen.
Glucocerebrosidase deficiency is Gaucher disease. It causes hepatosplenomegaly with crumpled tissue-paper macrophages but not a cherry-red spot.
Correct.
Galactocerebrosidase deficiency is Krabbe disease, an infantile leukodystrophy with globoid cells and peripheral neuropathy, without organ enlargement.

questions.stem: Electron microscopy of his cortical neurons shows lysosomes packed with concentric layers of membrane. Which of the following best explains the formation of this stored material?
options: Excess ganglioside synthesis in the endoplasmic reticulum
Failed peroxisomal oxidation of very long chain fatty acids
Impaired mitochondrial oxidation of myelin fatty acids
Blocked stepwise lysosomal breakdown of a sphingolipid
approach: Identify the storage site: lysosomes, so the problem is a failed lysosomal enzyme.
Recall that sphingolipids are broken down one sugar or group at a time, each step by its own lysosomal enzyme.
When one step fails, the substrate for that step piles up in membrane whorls.
questions.why: Gangliosides, cerebrosides, sulfatides, and sphingomyelin share a ceramide backbone and are broken down in lysosomes by a series of enzymes that each remove one piece. Synthesis is normal in these diseases. When one enzyme is missing, its substrate builds up as layered membrane whorls, and neurons swell and die. Myelin is rich in cholesterol, galactocerebroside, sulfatide, and sphingomyelin, so defects in their breakdown cause leukodystrophies, while ganglioside defects such as Tay-Sachs mainly damage neuronal cell bodies.
whyNot: Synthesis is normal in the sphingolipidoses. The problem is breakdown, which is why reducing synthesis is a treatment strategy.
Failed peroxisomal oxidation of these fatty acids is X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy. The material is not stored in lysosomes.
Mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation defects cause fasting hypoglycemia and muscle disease, not lysosomal membrane whorls.
Correct.

questions.stem: On light microscopy, his neuronal cell bodies are ballooned with stored lipid, and the normal basophilic Nissl substance is pushed to the edge of the cell. Which of the following best describes Nissl substance in a normal multipolar motor neuron?
options: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum concentrated in axon terminals
Rough endoplasmic reticulum absent from the axon hillock
Golgi stacks concentrated in the initial axon segment
Lysosome clusters filling the dendritic spines
approach: Recall what makes Nissl substance basophilic: RNA in ribosomes.
Nissl bodies are stacks of rough endoplasmic reticulum with free ribosomes.
They fill the soma and proximal dendrites but stop at the axon hillock, which is how the hillock is found on a slide.
questions.why: Neurons make large amounts of protein, so their soma and proximal dendrites are full of rough endoplasmic reticulum and ribosomes that stain blue with basic dyes. These are Nissl bodies. The axon hillock and axon lack them, so proteins needed in the axon are made in the soma and moved by axonal transport. A multipolar motor neuron has one axon and many dendrites. Dorsal root ganglion neurons are pseudounipolar, with one process that splits, and retinal and olfactory neurons are bipolar.
whyNot: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum lacks ribosomes and does not stain blue. Axon terminals hold synaptic vesicles and mitochondria.
Correct.
The Golgi apparatus sits in the soma near the nucleus. The initial axon segment is free of Nissl substance and holds clustered sodium channels.
Lysosomes are not basophilic, and dendritic spines contain actin and receptor clusters, not lysosome masses.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man has had burning pain in his hands and feet since childhood, reduced sweating, and clusters of small dark red papules between the umbilicus and knees. He has proteinuria and has just had an ischemic stroke. His maternal grandfather had kidney failure. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his disease?
approach: Group the clues: painful small fiber neuropathy, angiokeratomas, poor sweating, kidney disease, and early stroke.
This set is Fabry disease, where globotriaosylceramide builds up in nerves, vessel walls, and kidneys.
Fabry disease is X-linked, which fits disease passed through his mother's side.
questions.why: Fabry disease is an X-linked deficiency of alpha-galactosidase A. Globotriaosylceramide builds up in small nerve fibers, sweat glands, endothelium, kidney, and heart. This gives burning pain in the hands and feet, reduced sweating, angiokeratomas in the bathing-trunk area, proteinuria leading to kidney failure, cardiomyopathy, and early stroke. Gaucher types 2 and 3 involve the brain. Hurler (alpha-L-iduronidase, autosomal recessive) causes corneal clouding, while Hunter (iduronate-2-sulfatase, X-linked) does not.
whyNot: Correct.
Glucocerebrosidase deficiency is Gaucher disease, with hepatosplenomegaly, bone pain, and cytopenias. Neuronopathic types 2 and 3 cause brainstem signs, not painful neuropathy with angiokeratomas.
This is Hunter syndrome, an X-linked mucopolysaccharidosis with coarse facial features, joint stiffness, and in severe forms behavior problems, without corneal clouding.
This is Hurler syndrome, with coarse facial features, corneal clouding, and developmental decline in early childhood.

case: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the physician by her parents because of 6 months of irritability, impulsive spending, and falling grades. She now has a tremor of both arms that is worst when she holds them out, slurred speech, and drooling. Examination shows a coarse tremor of the outstretched arms, mild dystonic posturing of the left hand, and dysarthria. Slit-lamp examination shows a golden-brown ring at the edge of each cornea. Serum ceruloplasmin is 8 mg/dL (reference 20 to 50 mg/dL), 24-hour urine copper is 210 μg (reference less than 40 μg), and ALT is 78 U/L (reference 7 to 35 U/L). MRI shows bilateral T2 hyperintensity of the putamen. Diagnosis: Wilson disease.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the copper accumulation in her tissues?
options: Failed hepatocyte copper excretion into bile
Excess copper absorption by intestinal enterocytes
approach: Recall that bile is the main route for removing copper from the body.
Wilson disease is autosomal recessive loss of ATP7B, the copper-transporting ATPase of hepatocytes.
Without it, copper is neither excreted into bile nor loaded onto ceruloplasmin, so copper builds up in the liver and then spills into brain, cornea, and other tissues.
questions.why: ATP7B moves copper into the secretory pathway of hepatocytes, where it is loaded onto apoceruloplasmin and excreted into bile. When ATP7B fails, copper accumulates in the liver, causing hepatitis and cirrhosis. Free copper then leaks into the blood and deposits in the basal ganglia (tremor, dystonia, dysarthria, psychiatric change), the cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings), and the kidney. Apoceruloplasmin without copper is unstable, so serum ceruloplasmin is low, while urine copper rises.
whyNot: Correct.
Intestinal copper absorption is normal in Wilson disease. Defective copper transport out of enterocytes by ATP7A causes Menkes disease, which leads to copper deficiency.
Wilson disease is not autoimmune. Ceruloplasmin is low because it is not loaded with copper and is broken down faster.
Protein loss in nephrotic syndrome can lower ceruloplasmin, but it does not cause copper deposits in the brain or cornea.

questions.stem: Before her diagnosis, her physician considered another inherited disorder that causes psychiatric change and neuropathy in young adults. In that disorder, attacks bring severe abdominal pain, weakness, and anxiety, often after fasting or starting phenobarbital, without skin photosensitivity, and the urine darkens on standing in light. It is often inherited from one parent. Deficiency of which of the following enzymes causes that disorder?
approach: Recognize acute attacks of abdominal pain, neuropathy, and psychiatric symptoms triggered by fasting or drugs as acute intermittent porphyria.
No photosensitivity means the porphyrin rings are not building up, so the block is early in heme synthesis.
Dominant inheritance and buildup of porphobilinogen point to porphobilinogen deaminase.
questions.why: Acute intermittent porphyria is autosomal dominant partial deficiency of porphobilinogen deaminase (hydroxymethylbilane synthase). Triggers such as alcohol, fasting, and cytochrome P450 inducers like phenobarbital increase ALA synthase activity, so aminolevulinic acid and porphobilinogen pile up behind the block. These precursors are neurotoxic, causing abdominal pain, neuropathy, and psychiatric symptoms. Urine porphobilinogen is high and urine darkens in light. Treatment uses glucose and hemin, which suppress ALA synthase.
whyNot: This enzyme is deficient in porphyria cutanea tarda, which causes blistering skin on sun-exposed areas without neurologic attacks.
Ferrochelatase deficiency causes erythropoietic protoporphyria with painful skin photosensitivity. Lead also inhibits this enzyme.
Correct.
Lead poisoning inhibits this enzyme, and a rare recessive deficiency exists, but the dominant pattern and high porphobilinogen fit acute intermittent porphyria.

questions.stem: In a patient who died of untreated Wilson disease, the putamen shows loss of neurons, which have been replaced by a dense meshwork of cell processes that stain strongly for glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). Which of the following is another normal function of the cell type that formed this meshwork?
options: Formation of myelin around CNS axons
approach: GFAP is the intermediate filament of astrocytes, so the meshwork is a glial scar formed by reactive astrocytes.
List the other jobs of astrocytes: supporting the blood-brain barrier with their end-feet, buffering potassium, and recycling transmitters.
Match one of these to the options.
questions.why: When neurons die, astrocytes enlarge and lay down dense GFAP-filled processes, forming a glial scar (gliosis). In the healthy brain, astrocytes take up the potassium released by firing neurons and spread it through gap junctions, which keeps extracellular potassium stable. Their end-feet surround capillaries and support the tight junctions of the blood-brain barrier. They also take up glutamate and convert it to glutamine. In Wilson disease and liver failure, some astrocytes become swollen Alzheimer type II cells.
whyNot: Oligodendrocytes form CNS myelin. They do not form glial scars.
Microglia are the resident macrophages of the CNS. They derive from mesoderm and do not express GFAP.
Ependymal cells line the ventricles and central canal, and modified ependymal cells form the choroid plexus epithelium.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her parents describe her as previously cautious and organized. Over the past year she has made reckless purchases, made crude remarks to strangers, and shown little concern about failing her classes. Dysfunction of which of the following cortical regions best explains these behavioral changes?
approach: Group the changes: disinhibition, poor judgment, and lack of concern are personality and executive changes.
These functions belong to the prefrontal cortex, especially its orbitofrontal part.
The basal ganglia, damaged in her disease, form loops with the prefrontal cortex, so striatal injury can produce frontal-type behavior.
questions.why: The prefrontal cortex handles planning, judgment, impulse control, and social behavior. Orbitofrontal damage causes disinhibition and socially inappropriate behavior, while dorsolateral and medial damage cause poor planning and apathy. The caudate and putamen are part of loops that run from the prefrontal cortex through the basal ganglia and thalamus and back, so diseases of the striatum such as Wilson and Huntington disease often start with frontal-type behavior change. Frontotemporal dementia produces the same picture from direct frontal lobe degeneration.
whyNot: Superior parietal damage disturbs spatial awareness and visually guided reaching, not personality.
Correct.
The superior temporal gyrus holds auditory cortex and, on the left, Wernicke area. Damage causes hearing or language comprehension problems.
Precentral gyrus damage causes weakness on the opposite side, not behavior change.

dx: Lumbosacral myelomeningocele with Chiari II malformation and hydrocephalus
case: A newborn girl is examined shortly after delivery at 39 weeks' gestation. Her 23-year-old mother had no prenatal care and took no vitamins. A 4-cm open sac over the lower lumbar and sacral spine contains exposed neural tissue and leaks clear fluid. Both legs are flaccid with no movement, and the anal wink is absent. Her head circumference is 38 cm (above the 97th percentile), and the anterior fontanelle is full. MRI shows downward displacement of the cerebellar vermis and medulla through the foramen magnum, an elongated fourth ventricle, and enlarged lateral and third ventricles. Diagnosis: lumbosacral myelomeningocele with Chiari II malformation and hydrocephalus.

questions.stem: Failure of which of the following developmental events most directly caused her spinal lesion?
options: Notochord induction of the neural plate in week 3
Closure of the cranial neuropore in week 4
Segmentation of paraxial mesoderm into somites in week 5
Closure of the caudal neuropore in week 4
approach: An open sac with exposed neural tissue in the lumbosacral region is an open neural tube defect at the lower end.
Recall that the neural tube closes like a zipper from the middle, and the two ends close last.
The caudal (posterior) neuropore closes at about day 28, near the end of week 4.
questions.why: In week 3, the notochord induces the overlying ectoderm to thicken into the neural plate. The edges rise as neural folds and fuse in the midline, starting near the future neck and moving in both directions. The cranial neuropore closes at about day 25 and the caudal neuropore at about day 28. Failure of the caudal neuropore leaves the lower cord open, giving a myelomeningocele. Failure of the cranial neuropore gives anencephaly. Both happen before many people know they are pregnant.
whyNot: Failed induction of the neural plate would prevent the nervous system from forming. It is not the cause of a localized open lumbosacral defect.
Failure of the cranial neuropore causes anencephaly, not a lumbosacral defect.
Somite segmentation errors cause vertebral malformations such as hemivertebrae, not an open neural tube.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her mother plans another pregnancy in 2 years. Which of the following measures would most reduce the risk that a future child has a similar defect?
options: High-dose folic acid starting before conception
High-dose folic acid starting at 12 weeks of gestation
Iron supplements throughout the first trimester
approach: Recall that low folate before and in early pregnancy raises the risk of open neural tube defects.
The neural tube closes by the end of week 4, often before pregnancy is recognized.
Folic acid must already be in place when the tube is closing, so it has to start before conception.
questions.why: Folate supplies one-carbon units for nucleotide synthesis, which rapidly dividing neural tissue needs during neurulation. Women who have had a child with a neural tube defect are advised to take high-dose folic acid (about 4 mg a day) starting at least a month before conception and through the first trimester. All women who could become pregnant are advised to take about 0.4 mg a day. Open defects such as myelomeningocele and anencephaly leak alpha-fetoprotein into the amniotic fluid and maternal serum, so a high AFP is a screening clue. Spina bifida occulta is closed and does not raise AFP.
whyNot: Correct.
By 12 weeks the neural tube closed weeks earlier, so starting folic acid then is too late to prevent this defect.
B12 is needed to recycle folate, but supplementation is not the standard way to prevent recurrence of neural tube defects.
Iron prevents anemia in pregnancy but does not affect neural tube closure.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman has occipital headaches that worsen with coughing and straining. Examination shows loss of pain and temperature sensation over both shoulders and upper arms, with normal touch and position sense. Which of the following findings is most likely on her MRI?
options: Herniation of vermis and medulla with an elongated fourth ventricle
Vermis agenesis with cystic enlargement of the fourth ventricle
Tonsils below the foramen magnum with a cervical syrinx
Stenosis of the cerebral aqueduct with enlarged third ventricle
approach: Cape-like loss of pain and temperature with spared touch points to a syrinx damaging the crossing spinothalamic fibers in the cervical cord.
Headache worse with coughing in an adult suggests crowding at the foramen magnum.
Together these fit Chiari I malformation, which is often linked to syringomyelia.
questions.why: Chiari I malformation is downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils below the foramen magnum. It often presents in adults with occipital headache worsened by coughing or straining. It disturbs CSF flow and is commonly associated with a cervical syrinx that damages the fibers crossing in the anterior white commissure, causing cape-like loss of pain and temperature. Chiari II, as in the infant, involves the vermis and medulla, presents at birth, and comes with lumbosacral myelomeningocele and hydrocephalus. Dandy-Walker malformation is vermis agenesis with a cystic fourth ventricle.
whyNot: This is Chiari II malformation, seen in infants with lumbosacral myelomeningocele.
This is Dandy-Walker malformation, which presents in infancy with an enlarging head and hydrocephalus.
Correct.
Aqueductal stenosis causes noncommunicating hydrocephalus with headache and papilledema, but it does not explain cape-like sensory loss.

topics: Chiari I, Chiari II, and Dandy-Walker malformations

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains her enlarged head and full anterior fontanelle?
options: Communicating hydrocephalus from scarred arachnoid granulations
Noncommunicating hydrocephalus in a skull that can expand
Hydrocephalus ex vacuo from loss of brain tissue
Overproduction of CSF by a choroid plexus tumor
approach: In Chiari II, the herniated hindbrain blocks outflow from the fourth ventricle, and aqueductal stenosis is common.
A block inside the ventricular system is noncommunicating hydrocephalus.
In an infant the sutures are not fused, so rising pressure enlarges the head and makes the fontanelle full.
questions.why: Hydrocephalus is too much CSF with enlarged ventricles. In noncommunicating hydrocephalus, flow is blocked within the ventricles, as with aqueductal stenosis, Chiari II, Dandy-Walker malformation, or a tumor. In communicating hydrocephalus, CSF reaches the subarachnoid space but is poorly absorbed, often after meningitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage scars the arachnoid granulations. Before the sutures fuse, raised pressure spreads the skull bones, so head circumference grows quickly. In older children and adults the skull is rigid, so pressure rises and causes headache, vomiting, and papilledema.
whyNot: Arachnoid granulation scarring follows meningitis or subarachnoid hemorrhage. Neither is present here, and her block is within the ventricles.
Correct.
Hydrocephalus ex vacuo is ventricular enlargement after brain tissue loss, as in Alzheimer disease. Pressure is normal, and the head does not enlarge.
A choroid plexus papilloma can overproduce CSF, but her MRI shows a hindbrain malformation and no tumor.

dx: Medulloblastoma of the cerebellar vermis with obstructive hydrocephalus
case: A 6-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of 3 weeks of morning headaches and vomiting and a week of frequent falls. His temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 52/min, respirations are 10/min and irregular, and blood pressure is 156/94 mm Hg. Examination shows bilateral papilledema and a wide-based, unsteady gait. MRI shows a 4-cm enhancing midline mass arising from the cerebellar vermis and filling the fourth ventricle, with obstructive hydrocephalus. After urgent CSF diversion, the mass is resected. Microscopy shows sheets of small cells with scant cytoplasm and dark nuclei, some arranged in rings around central fibrillary material. Diagnosis: medulloblastoma.

questions.stem: As part of staging, MRI of the entire spine and lumbar CSF cytology are obtained. Which of the following best explains why these studies are needed?
options: Hematogenous spread to the vertebral marrow
Seeding through the CSF onto spinal meninges
Lymphatic spread to the cervical lymph nodes
Direct invasion down the spinal cord parenchyma
approach: Recall that medulloblastoma grows into the fourth ventricle and is bathed in CSF.
Tumor cells shed into the CSF and settle on the leptomeninges of the spinal cord and cauda equina (drop metastases).
Staging therefore needs imaging of the whole neuraxis and CSF cytology.
questions.why: Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor of childhood. It is an embryonal small round blue cell tumor of the cerebellum, usually the vermis, and Homer Wright rosettes (tumor cells around a core of fibrils) are typical. Because it projects into the fourth ventricle, it can block CSF flow and shed cells into the CSF. These cells seed the spinal leptomeninges as drop metastases, which changes treatment to include craniospinal radiation. It is highly radiosensitive.
whyNot: Spread outside the CNS is uncommon. Spinal disease comes from CSF seeding, not blood-borne marrow metastasis.
Correct.
Brain tumors rarely spread through lymphatics to lymph nodes, so nodal disease is not the staging concern.
Medulloblastoma does not grow down through cord tissue. It reaches the spine by floating in the CSF.

questions.stem: Before surgery, the main alternative diagnosis was the other common posterior fossa tumor of children, which often appears as a cyst with an enhancing mural nodule in a cerebellar hemisphere. Which of the following pairs of findings is typical of that tumor?
options: Psammoma bodies with NF2 gene loss
Rosenthal fibers with a BRAF alteration
approach: A cystic cerebellar tumor with a mural nodule in a child is a pilocytic astrocytoma.
Recall its histology: piloid (hair-like) astrocytes, Rosenthal fibers, and eosinophilic granular bodies.
Recall its genetics: an activating BRAF alteration, most often a KIAA1549-BRAF fusion.
questions.why: Pilocytic astrocytoma is the most common brain tumor of children overall. It is usually a well-circumscribed cystic tumor with a mural nodule in the cerebellum, and it has a good prognosis after resection. Microscopy shows bipolar hair-like astrocytes and Rosenthal fibers, which are dense eosinophilic GFAP-rich bodies. Most carry a BRAF alteration that activates MAPK signaling. Diffuse gliomas in adults differ: oligodendroglioma is IDH-mutant with 1p/19q codeletion and fried-egg cells, often in the frontal lobe with seizures and calcification.
whyNot: These define oligodendroglioma, a diffuse glioma of adults that usually arises in the frontal lobe and presents with seizures.
These fit meningioma, a dural-based tumor of adults, often women. Bilateral vestibular schwannomas and meningiomas suggest NF2.
These fit glioblastoma, the most common primary malignant brain tumor of older adults, usually in the cerebral hemispheres.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains his slow pulse at presentation?
options: Baroreflex slowing after a sympathetic pressor surge
Direct compression of the vagus nerve by the tumor
Reduced venous return from raised intrathoracic pressure
approach: Recognize the Cushing triad: hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular breathing with raised intracranial pressure.
Cerebral perfusion pressure equals mean arterial pressure minus intracranial pressure, so a high ICP lowers perfusion of the brainstem.
The ischemic brainstem triggers a sympathetic surge that raises blood pressure, and the baroreceptors then slow the heart through the vagus.
questions.why: As intracranial pressure rises, cerebral perfusion pressure (MAP minus ICP) falls. The brainstem responds with intense sympathetic output that raises arterial pressure and restores perfusion. Carotid sinus and aortic baroreceptors sense the high pressure and increase vagal output to the heart, slowing it. Compression of the medulla also makes breathing irregular. Normally, autoregulation keeps cerebral blood flow steady across a wide range of pressures, and PaCO2 changes vessel tone, with high CO2 dilating and low CO2 constricting cerebral arterioles.
whyNot: Correct.
Compression of the vagus nerve would interrupt vagal output and tend to speed the heart. Here the slowing is a reflex response to the high blood pressure.
Hypercapnia dilates cerebral vessels and raises ICP further, but it does not explain the combination of bradycardia with marked hypertension.
Low venous return would lower blood pressure and speed the heart. His blood pressure is high.

questions.stem: Which of the following sets of CSF spaces is most likely dilated by the obstruction in this patient?
options: Lateral and third ventricles plus the aqueduct
All four ventricles and the subarachnoid cisterns
approach: Trace CSF flow: lateral ventricles, interventricular foramina, third ventricle, cerebral aqueduct, fourth ventricle, then the foramina of Luschka and Magendie.
Locate the block: the tumor fills the fourth ventricle.
Every space upstream of the block dilates.
questions.why: CSF is made mainly by the choroid plexus in the lateral ventricles. It passes through the interventricular foramina of Monro to the third ventricle, down the cerebral aqueduct to the fourth ventricle, and out through the median foramen of Magendie and the lateral foramina of Luschka into the subarachnoid space. A mass filling the fourth ventricle blocks flow at that level, so the lateral ventricles, third ventricle, and aqueduct all enlarge. Aqueductal stenosis spares the fourth ventricle, and a block at one foramen of Monro enlarges only one lateral ventricle.
whyNot: Only one lateral ventricle dilates when one interventricular foramen is blocked, as by a colloid cyst or other mass at the foramen.
This pattern fits aqueductal stenosis. With the block in the fourth ventricle, the aqueduct also dilates.
Correct.
Enlargement of all four ventricles fits communicating hydrocephalus or a block at the fourth ventricle outflow foramina.

case: A 2-year-old girl is brought to the physician because her parents felt a hard lump in her abdomen while bathing her. She has had poor appetite, weight loss, and bruising around both eyes for 3 weeks. Examination shows a firm, irregular, nontender mass in the left upper quadrant that extends past the midline, and bilateral periorbital ecchymoses. CT shows a 9-cm left adrenal mass with calcifications that surrounds the aorta. Urine homovanillic acid and vanillylmandelic acid are elevated. Biopsy shows sheets of small round blue cells with scattered rosettes around central fibrillary material. Diagnosis: neuroblastoma of the left adrenal gland.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings in her tumor would most strongly predict aggressive behavior and a poor prognosis?
options: Biallelic loss of the RB1 gene
Activating fusion of the BRAF gene
approach: Identify the tumor: a neural crest tumor of the adrenal medulla in a young child with high HVA and VMA is neuroblastoma.
Recall the key molecular marker used for risk grouping in neuroblastoma.
Many extra copies of the MYCN oncogene drive rapid growth and predict a poor outcome.
questions.why: Neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid tumor of young children. It arises from neural crest cells of the adrenal medulla or sympathetic chain and often presents as an abdominal mass that crosses the midline, unlike Wilms tumor. Spread to the orbit gives periorbital bruising, and some children have opsoclonus-myoclonus. MYCN amplification, found in about a fifth of cases, marks high-risk disease regardless of stage. Younger age at diagnosis and favorable histology predict a better course, and some infant tumors regress on their own.
whyNot: Two-hit RB1 loss causes retinoblastoma, which presents with leukocoria.
This codeletion, with IDH mutation, defines oligodendroglioma and predicts a better response to treatment.
Correct.
BRAF alterations are typical of pilocytic astrocytoma in children, which has a good prognosis.

questions.stem: Her elevated urine homovanillic acid reflects breakdown of which of the following monoamines, by which enzymes?
approach: Recall the end product of each monoamine: dopamine gives homovanillic acid, norepinephrine and epinephrine give vanillylmandelic acid, and serotonin gives 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid.
Recall the enzymes: monoamine oxidase removes the amine group and catechol-O-methyltransferase methylates the ring.
Homovanillic acid needs both steps applied to dopamine.
questions.why: Catecholamines are broken down by two enzymes that can act in either order. Monoamine oxidase (MAO) oxidizes the amine, and catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) adds a methyl group to the catechol ring. Dopamine is converted to homovanillic acid. Norepinephrine and epinephrine are converted to metanephrines by COMT and then to vanillylmandelic acid. Neuroblastoma cells make large amounts of dopamine and norepinephrine, so both urine HVA and VMA are high, which helps with diagnosis and follow-up.
whyNot: Norepinephrine broken down by MAO and COMT gives vanillylmandelic acid, not homovanillic acid.
Correct.
Serotonin is not a catecholamine. MAO converts it to 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid, which is high in carcinoid syndrome.
COMT acting alone on epinephrine gives metanephrine, which is high in pheochromocytoma.

questions.stem: Which of the following pairs of cells share the embryologic origin of the cells that gave rise to her tumor?
options: Adrenal cortical cells and ovarian stromal cells
Schwann cells and dorsal root ganglion neurons
approach: Identify the cell of origin: chromaffin precursors of the adrenal medulla.
Recall that the adrenal medulla comes from neural crest, while the adrenal cortex comes from mesoderm.
Find the pair of cells that also come from neural crest.
questions.why: Neural crest cells leave the edges of the neural folds as the tube closes and migrate widely. They form dorsal root, cranial sensory, and autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla, melanocytes, and parts of the face and heart outflow tract. The neural tube itself (neuroectoderm) forms CNS neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, ependyma, and the retina. Microglia come from mesoderm, from yolk sac precursors related to the monocyte line.
whyNot: Oligodendrocytes and astrocytes come from neuroectoderm of the neural tube, not from neural crest.
Microglia and monocytes come from mesoderm.
The adrenal cortex and gonadal stroma both come from intermediate mesoderm. Only the adrenal medulla comes from neural crest.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her tumor arose from precursors of adrenal chromaffin cells. In a healthy person, which of the following receptors on chromaffin cells triggers catecholamine release during sympathetic activation?
options: Nicotinic receptor with a cation channel
Muscarinic M3 receptor coupled to Gq protein
Alpha-2 adrenergic receptor coupled to Gi
Beta-1 adrenergic receptor coupled to Gs
approach: Recall that chromaffin cells act as modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons.
They are directly innervated by preganglionic sympathetic fibers, which release acetylcholine.
At every autonomic ganglion-type synapse, acetylcholine acts on nicotinic receptors, which are ligand-gated cation channels.
questions.why: All preganglionic autonomic neurons release acetylcholine onto nicotinic receptors, which are ligand-gated channels that let sodium in and depolarize the cell. Chromaffin cells receive preganglionic sympathetic fibers directly from the splanchnic nerves, so they are stimulated the same way and release epinephrine and some norepinephrine into the blood. Postganglionic sympathetic neurons release norepinephrine onto adrenergic receptors: alpha-1 uses Gq, alpha-2 uses Gi, and beta receptors use Gs. Postganglionic parasympathetic neurons, and sympathetic neurons to sweat glands, release acetylcholine onto muscarinic receptors: M1 and M3 use Gq, and M2 uses Gi.
whyNot: Correct.
M3 receptors are on parasympathetic targets such as glands and smooth muscle, and on sweat glands. They do not trigger adrenal medullary release.
Alpha-2 receptors are mainly presynaptic and inhibit transmitter release through Gi.
Beta-1 receptors on the heart and kidney respond to catecholamines. They do not drive chromaffin cell secretion.

case: A 63-year-old woman comes to the physician because of 5 weeks of morning headaches and trouble recognizing people. She does not know her own husband or children until they speak, although she names objects and reads normally. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows mild papilledema and no weakness or sensory loss. MRI shows a 5-cm mass in the right inferior occipitotemporal lobe, including the fusiform gyrus, with an irregular enhancing rim around a necrotic center and extensive surrounding T2 hyperintensity in the white matter. Stereotactic biopsy shows a highly cellular astrocytic tumor that stains for GFAP. Molecular testing shows wildtype IDH. Diagnosis: glioblastoma.

questions.stem: Which of the following additional histologic findings is most likely in her biopsy?
approach: A ring-enhancing, necrotic hemispheric astrocytic tumor in an older adult with wildtype IDH is glioblastoma.
Recall its defining features: necrosis with pseudopalisading tumor cells and microvascular proliferation.
Match the other options to meningioma, oligodendroglioma, and ependymoma.
questions.why: Glioblastoma is the most common primary malignant brain tumor in adults. It is a diffuse astrocytic tumor, IDH-wildtype in most cases, that stains for GFAP. Its diagnostic features are necrosis bordered by lined-up tumor cells (pseudopalisading) and microvascular proliferation, which make the irregular enhancing rim seen on MRI. It infiltrates along white matter tracts and can cross the corpus callosum to the other hemisphere, giving a butterfly pattern. Median survival is only about 15 months with treatment.
whyNot: Correct.
Whorls and psammoma bodies are typical of meningioma, an extra-axial dural tumor of arachnoid cells that is GFAP negative.
These are features of oligodendroglioma, which is IDH-mutant with 1p/19q codeletion.
Perivascular pseudorosettes mark ependymoma, which in children usually arises in the fourth ventricle.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man has a slowly growing, calcified frontal lobe tumor that presents with a seizure. Its cells have round nuclei with clear cytoplasm, and the tumor lies among a network of branching capillaries. Which of the following molecular findings is most likely in his tumor, in contrast to hers?
options: Biallelic loss of the RB1 tumor suppressor gene
Activating fusion of the BRAF kinase gene
approach: Identify his tumor: a calcified frontal tumor with fried-egg cells and chicken-wire capillaries in a younger adult with seizures is oligodendroglioma.
Recall that oligodendroglioma is defined by an IDH mutation plus whole-arm loss of 1p and 19q.
Her glioblastoma is IDH-wildtype, which separates the two.
questions.why: Mutant IDH1 or IDH2 makes the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate, which alters DNA and histone methylation and drives some diffuse gliomas. Oligodendroglioma requires both an IDH mutation and codeletion of chromosome arms 1p and 19q. It grows slowly, responds better to treatment, and has a longer survival than glioblastoma. Other driver genes in nervous system tumors include two-hit RB1 loss in retinoblastoma and MYCN amplification in aggressive neuroblastoma.
whyNot: Two-hit RB1 loss causes retinoblastoma in young children, not a frontal glioma in an adult.
MYCN amplification predicts aggressive neuroblastoma, a neural crest tumor of young children.
Correct.
BRAF fusions are typical of pilocytic astrocytoma, usually a cystic cerebellar tumor in children.

questions.stem: She can reach for and pick up objects accurately and can judge the direction of moving cars. Damage to which of the following pathways best explains her inability to recognize faces?
options: Arcuate fasciculus to the frontal lobe
Optic radiation through the parietal lobe
approach: Name the deficit: inability to recognize familiar faces with normal vision is prosopagnosia.
Recall the two visual association streams leaving the occipital lobe: dorsal (where and how) and ventral (what and who).
Face recognition depends on the fusiform gyrus in the ventral stream, which her tumor involves.
questions.why: From primary visual cortex, the dorsal stream runs to the parietal lobe and handles where objects are, how they move, and how to reach for them. The ventral stream runs along the inferior temporal lobe and handles recognizing objects, colors, and faces. The fusiform gyrus contains a face-selective area, and damage there, especially on the right or on both sides, causes prosopagnosia. Patients still know people by voice or gait. Her intact reaching and motion judgment show that the dorsal stream is spared.
whyNot: Dorsal stream damage disturbs spatial location, motion perception, and visually guided reaching, which are normal in her.
Correct.
The arcuate fasciculus connects Wernicke and Broca areas. Damage causes conduction aphasia with poor repetition.
Damage to the upper optic radiation in the parietal lobe causes a contralateral inferior quadrantanopia, not loss of face recognition.

questions.stem: She is started on dexamethasone, and within days her headache improves and the T2 hyperintensity around the tumor shrinks. Which of the following mechanisms best explains the fluid seen around her tumor?
options: Failure of neuronal Na+/K+ ATPase from ischemia
Transependymal flow of CSF from blocked ventricles
Osmotic water shift after a rapid fall in serum sodium
Leaky tumor vessels letting plasma into white matter
approach: Note the setting: edema around a tumor that spreads through the white matter and responds to corticosteroids.
Tumor vessels lack a normal blood-brain barrier, so plasma leaks out and tracks along white matter fibers.
This is vasogenic edema; corticosteroids tighten the leaky vessels.
questions.why: Vasogenic edema forms when the blood-brain barrier breaks down, as with tumors, abscesses, and trauma. Protein-rich fluid leaks into the extracellular space and spreads easily through white matter, which is why it looks like finger-like T2 hyperintensity around the mass. Corticosteroids reduce this leak. Cytotoxic edema is swelling of cells when ATP-dependent pumps fail in ischemia, and it affects gray and white matter alike. Interstitial edema comes from CSF pushed across the ependyma in hydrocephalus. Any edema raises intracranial pressure and can cause papilledema, the Cushing triad, and herniation.
